A 34-year-old woman comes to the office due to dyspnea, lower extremity edema, and fatigue that have progressively worsened over the past 4 weeks.  The patient has had no chest pain, palpitations, or syncope.  She has no chronic medical conditions but reports a self-resolving upper respiratory illness 2 months ago.  The patient does not use tobacco, alcohol, or recreational drugs and takes no medications.  There is no history of cardiovascular disease in her family.  Physical examination is notable for bilateral lung crackles and lower extremity edema.  Echocardiography reveals normal valve function but generalized hypokinesis and chamber enlargement with decreased ventricular systolic function.  Compared to her previous normal state of health (represented by Point X in the graph below), which of the following changes in cardiac hemodynamics has most likely occurred in this patient?

​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​
explanation:
This patient's progressive dyspnea and fatigue, lung crackles (ie, pulmonary edema), and lower extremity edema are consistent with decompensated heart failure.  Her young age and recent upper respiratory illness suggest viral cardiomyopathy as the underlying etiology.

Cardiac function–vascular function curves demonstrate the interdependent relationship between cardiac output and venous return.

  • The cardiac function curve is essentially a Frank-Starling curve, representing constant left ventricular contractility (inotropy) along the curve.  Increased contractility shifts the curve upward/left, whereas decreased contractility shifts it downward/right.

  • The vascular function curve represents venous return to the right atrium.  Changes in blood volume, venous capacitance, or systemic vascular resistance (SVR) shift the curve upward/left or downward/right.

  • The intersection point of the curves represents the steady-state right atrial pressure and cardiac output for a given set of cardiac and vascular parameters.

This patient's echocardiography shows reduced left ventricular systolic function, indicating reduced contractility that shifts the cardiac function curve to the right.  In addition, increased retention of sodium and water occurs with decompensated heart failure, resulting in increased blood volume (ie, increased venous return) that shifts the vascular function curve to the right.  A new steady-state equilibrium is reached at an increased right atrial pressure and reduced cardiac output.

(Choices A and D)  A shift to Point A or Point D represents a change in venous return with no change in contractility.  The shift to Point A (increased venous return) could occur with infusion of normal saline, and the shift to Point D (decreased venous return) could occur with dehydration (cardiac output increases or decreases, respectively, according to the Frank-Starling law).

(Choice C)  A shift to Point C represents decreased contractility and decreased venous return, as may be seen in a patient who develops systolic heart failure and is given a dose of nitroglycerin (ie, increased venous capacitance).  However, this patient would be expected to have increased venous return due to fluid retention from heart failure.

(Choice E)  A shift to Point E represents increased contractility and decreased venous return, as could occur with early sepsis (blood volume decreases due to leaky vasculature, and there is a sympathetically mediated increase in contractility).

(Choice F)  A shift to Point F represents increased cardiac output and increased venous return, as could be seen with the increase in contractility and decrease in SVR that occur with exercise.

Educational objective:Decompensated heart failure due to systolic dysfunction involves reduced contractility to shift the cardiac function curve to the right, and increased blood volume to shift the venous return curve to the right.  This results in a new equilibrium point at an increased right atrial pressure and reduced cardiac output.​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​
